title: Macbeth
question: Reread Lady Macbeth's line below. How does she use the idea of being "a man" to push Macbeth toward the murder? Support your answer with one detail from Scene 7. “When you durst do it, then you were a man”
model_answer: Lady Macbeth defines manhood as daring to act on what one wants, so Macbeth's hesitation becomes a loss of manhood. She reminds him that he was "a man" when he first proposed the plan and calls him a coward "in thine own esteem" who lets "I dare not" wait upon "I would." Macbeth replies that a true man knows limits ("Who dares do more is none"), but by the end of the scene he is "settled."
rubric_2: Explains that she links manhood to daring or acting on desire, so backing out makes him less of a man or a coward, AND supports it with a relevant detail from Scene 7 (the coward taunt, the cat proverb, the babe image, Macbeth's reply about what becomes a man, or his final "I am settled").
rubric_1: Says she insults or pressures him but does not explain the link between manhood and daring, OR gives an accurate reading with no supporting detail.
rubric_0: Misreads the line (for example, says she praises his restraint or means only courage in battle) or does not address it.
evidence: When you durst do it, then you were a man; And, to be more than what you were, you would Be so much more the man. … And live a coward in thine own esteem, Letting "I dare not" wait upon "I would," … I dare do all that may become a man; Who dares do more is none. … I am settled, and bend up Each corporal agent to this terrible feat.

title: Macbeth
question: Reread Lady Macbeth's line below. How does it answer what Macbeth said about his bloody hand while she was away? Support your answer with his image from Scene 2. “A little water clears us of this deed: How easy is it then!”
model_answer: Lady Macbeth treats the blood as a practical problem that "a little water" will solve. Moments before, alone, Macbeth asked whether "all great Neptune's ocean" could wash the blood from his hand and answered that his hand would rather turn "the multitudinous seas" red. rubric_2: Contrasts her view (the blood and the deed wash off easily) with his (no water can clean it) AND cites Macbeth's specific image: Neptune's ocean that cannot wash his hand, or his hand turning the seas red ("incarnadine," "making the green one red").
rubric_1: Explains that she downplays the guilt or contrasts it with his guilt in general terms, without his ocean or seas image.
rubric_0: Misreads the line (for example, says she feels guilty or afraid) or does not address it.
evidence: Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood Clean from my hand? No, this my hand will rather The multitudinous seas incarnadine, Making the green one red. … My hands are of your color, but I shame To wear a heart so white. … A little water clears us of this deed: How easy is it then!

title: Macbeth
question: Reread Macbeth's words to the murderers below. What remark is he answering, and what does he challenge the murderers to prove? Support your answer with one detail from Scene 1. “Ay, in the catalogue ye go for men; As hounds, and greyhounds, mongrels, spaniels, curs,”
model_answer: Macbeth is answering the First Murderer's protest, "We are men, my liege," after he asks whether they will let Banquo's wrongs go. He replies that all dogs share one name but differ in worth; in the same way, being called men proves nothing. He challenges them to show they have "a station in the file, Not i' th' worst rank of manhood" by killing Banquo. Stung, the murderers answer that they are reckless enough to do anything to spite the world.
rubric_2: Explains that Macbeth says the name "men" proves nothing, just as all dogs are called dogs, and challenges them to prove their worth by killing Banquo, AND gives a specific Scene 1 detail: the First Murderer's "We are men, my liege," the "worst rank of manhood" challenge, or the murderers' replies about being reckless or weary of the world.
rubric_1: Says he insults or flatters them into the murder without explaining the dog comparison, OR explains it with no specific detail from the scene.
rubric_0: Misreads the passage (for example, says he is describing his hunting dogs or praising the murderers) or does not address it.
evidence: We are men, my liege. … Now, if you have a station in the file, Not i' th' worst rank of manhood, say't; … I am one, my liege, Whom the vile blows and buffets of the world Hath so incens'd that I am reckless what I do to spite the world.

title: Macbeth
question: Reread Lady Macduff's words below. What is she saying about her husband's flight, and how does Ross answer her charge? Support your answer with one detail from Scene 2. “for the poor wren, The most diminutive of birds, will fight, Her young ones in her nest, against the owl.”
model_answer: Lady Macduff says that even the tiny wren fights the owl to protect her young, yet her husband has fled and left his family; he "wants the natural touch" and acted from fear, not love. Ross defends Macduff: she cannot know "whether it was his wisdom or his fear," and her husband is "noble, wise, judicious" and understands "the fits o' th' season." He hints that the times are so cruel that men are called traitors without knowing why, but dares not say more.
rubric_2: Explains the wren comparison (even the smallest bird defends its young, so Macduff's flight shows a lack of natural love or courage) AND gives Ross's answer with a specific detail: "wisdom or his fear," "noble, wise, judicious," "best knows the fits o' th' season," or "cruel are the times, when we are traitors."

rubric_0: Misreads the passage (for example, says she praises her husband's courage) or does not address it.
evidence: He loves us not: He wants the natural touch; … You know not Whether it was his wisdom or his fear. … but, for your husband, He is noble, wise, judicious, and best knows The fits o' th' season. … But cruel are the times, when we are traitors, And do not know ourselves;

title: Macbeth
question: Reread Angus's image below. What does it suggest about Macbeth as king? Support your answer with the other image of clothing that a Scottish lord uses for Macbeth earlier in Scene 2. “now does he feel his title Hang loose about him, like a giant's robe Upon a dwarfish thief.”
model_answer: Angus pictures the crown as a giant's robe stolen by a dwarf: the title is too big for Macbeth, does not fit him, and was never his to wear. rubric_0: Misreads the image (for example, says Macbeth is growing into his role or is a giant among men) or does not address it.
evidence: He cannot buckle his distemper'd cause Within the belt of rule. … now does he feel his title Hang loose about him, like a giant's robe Upon a dwarfish thief.
